Neonates of the Mongolia rock agama hatch from eggs that measure approximately 2.5 centimeters [Lb = approximately 2.5 centimeters] in snout–vent length at hatching, a modest size consistent with the pattern observed in other agamid lizards such as Calotes versicolor upon which these estimates are partially based. Newly emerged juveniles are immediately reliant on their yolk reserves and rapidly commence exogenous feeding within days of emergence, actively pursuing small arthropod prey among the rocky outcrops of their montane habitat. The hatchlings exhibit cryptic coloration that closely matches the granitic substrate, affording them some protection from avian predators during this vulnerable early stage. Within the first weeks of life, growth rates are relatively rapid as the young individuals exploit the brief, warm summer season to accumulate body mass and increase in linear dimensions before the onset of winter dormancy. This initial snout–vent length of 2.5 centimeters [Lb = 2.5 centimeters] is typical for agamids of comparable adult size and sets the foundation for subsequent ontogenetic development, which will eventually lead to the attainment of reproductive maturity over the following years under the prevailing thermal conditions of their high-altitude environment.

Adult females of Paralaudakia stoliczkana typically attain a maximum snout–vent length of 13.1 centimeters [Li = 13.1 centimeters], while adult males grow to a slightly larger ultimate size of 14.3 centimeters [Li = 14.3 centimeters] in snout–vent length, a modest degree of sexual dimorphism that is common among agamid lizards. The larger body size in males likely confers advantages during intrasexual competition for territories and access to receptive females, as male-male agonistic encounters involving head-bobbing displays and lateral compression are frequently observed during the breeding season. Females, however, may benefit from achieving a robust body size as well, as larger females can carry more yolk-laden eggs and produce larger clutch sizes, thereby potentially enhancing their lifetime reproductive output. Body mass at this asymptotic stage reaches about 69.3 grams [Wwi = about 69.3 grams] of wet weight, a value that reflects the relatively compact, heavy-bodied build of this saxicolous species. Studies based on field-captured adults suggest that this ultimate wet body mass is achieved gradually over several growing seasons, with individuals investing substantial resources into skeletal growth before somatic mass reaches its plateau. The slight difference in ultimate snout–vent lengths between sexes is maintained across the populations studied, indicating a consistent pattern of male-biased dimorphism in this taxon.

Sexual maturation in the Mongolia rock agama is attained when juveniles reach a snout–vent length of approximately 9.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 9.5 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the initiation of gonadal activity and the onset of reproductive competence. This pubertal size is reached after a period of approximately 5 years since birth [tp = approximately 5 years since birth] when the animals are maintained under standard laboratory thermal conditions at a constant temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], reflecting the relatively slow pace of life characteristic of a high-altitude, seasonally constrained environment. In the wild, where temperatures fluctuate widely and the active season is limited to a few months each year, the time since birth at puberty may be somewhat extended, although direct field validation remains scarce. The attainment of a snout–vent length of 9.5 centimeters [Lp = 9.5 centimeters] is a reliable morphological indicator that an individual has transitioned from the juvenile growth phase into the reproductively viable segment of the population, capable of engaging in courtship and egg production in subsequent breeding seasons. Once this size is reached, individuals typically continue to grow for several additional years before approaching their asymptotic dimensions.

Females that have attained the pubertal snout–vent length of 9.5 centimeters [Lp = 9.5 centimeters] are capable of producing up to 10 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = up to 10 eggs per clutch] and may produce two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year] under favorable conditions at a stable temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], leading to an impressive maximum annual reproductive output. Each clutch is deposited in a shallow scrape excavated in sandy soil beneath a sun-warmed boulder, where the parchment-shelled eggs are left to incubate for an extended period. The eggs themselves are relatively large for an agamid of this body size, drawing heavily on the female's limited energy reserves, especially when two clutches are produced in a single active season. Gravid females are noticeably distended and often reduce their movement and feeding activity in the days leading up to oviposition, presumably to minimize the risk of predation during this vulnerable state. The capacity to produce 10 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 10 eggs per clutch] twice annually [F_R_i = twice annually] represents a high fecundity for a lizard inhabiting a resource-limited, high-altitude ecosystem, and may reflect a compensatory life-history strategy for relatively high juvenile mortality during the harsh winters.

Embryonic development proceeds relatively slowly, with eggs maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] requiring approximately 52.5 days [ab = approximately 52.5 days] to complete development before the leathery eggshell is pipped and the neonate emerges. This incubation period, equivalent to about seven and a half weeks of constant warmth, is typical for agamid lizards kept at moderate temperatures and reflects the energy-conserving pace of development in a species adapted to cool montane environments. Once hatched, the young face a brief window of favorable weather in which to feed and grow before their first winter hibernation. The oldest documented individuals in captivity have survived for as long as 9 years [am = 9 years] when maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], suggesting a lifespan far exceeding that of many small-bodied agamids and indicative of a relatively slow life-history pace. This longevity, combined with the extended time required to reach reproductive maturity, means that an individual may have only a limited number of breeding seasons in which to contribute offspring to the next generation, placing a premium on each successful nesting attempt.
